The numbers $a$ and $b$ are the coordinates of $\vec{w}$ in that basis. The usual basis, $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$, is merely the most convenient; with any other, the coordinates are worked out by solving a [[al-sistemas|system]] of two equations.

El producto escalar da dos herramientas:: The dot product gives two tools: the sign, which classifies the angle for free, and zero, which detects perpendicularity. The exact angle is only needed when it is asked for.
El producto escalar mide «cuánto va en l: The dot product measures “how much goes the same way”, and from that come two constant uses. In physics it is work: pushing a trolley forwards tires you out, pushing it at the floor does not move it, and the formula takes care of that by itself because the cosine of 90° is zero. In computing it is how a 3D scene is lit: the brightness of each point is worked out with the dot product between the surface normal and the direction of the light.
El producto escalar pone número a esa id: The dot product puts a number to that idea. It comes out positive if the two vectors point more or less the same way, zero if they are perpendicular and negative if they point opposite ways. From the sign alone you already know which situation you are in, without working out any angle.
El punto entre los vectores se lee «prod:
The dot between the vectors is read “dot product”: $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}$ is “u dot v”, never “u times v”.

They read: “u dot v equals u one times v one, plus u two times v two” · “u dot v equals the magnitude of u, times the magnitude of v, times the cosine of alpha” · “cosine of alpha equals u one v one plus u two v two, over the magnitude of u times the magnitude of v”.

$\alpha$ is the Greek letter alpha and here it is the angle the two vectors make.
El vector que va del punto $A(a_1,a_2)$: The vector going from the point $A(a_1,a_2)$ to the point $B(b_1,b_2)$ is worked out by subtracting: finish minus start.
Es <em>final menos inicial</em>: $B - A$: It is finish minus start: $B - A$. The other way round gives the vector pointing the opposite way.
Es un número. Multiplicar componente a c: It is a number. Multiply component by component and add: $(3, 1)\cdot(2, 5) = 6 + 5 = 11$, not $(6, 5)$.
Ese coseno del producto escalar tiene un: That cosine in the dot product has a relative that solves triangles with no right angles. The [[tr-teoremas|cosine rule]] is literally what comes out of expanding $|\vec u - \vec v|^2$ with the formula above: good old Pythagoras plus a correction term worth $-2|\vec u||\vec v|\cos\alpha$ that disappears exactly when the angle is right. It is worth doing that calculation once.
Eso es $A - B$: el vector que va de $B$: That is $A - B$: the vector going from $B$ to $A$, that is, $\vec{BA}$. It points the opposite way.
Eso es el producto escalar. La sombra se: That is the dot product. The shadow is obtained by dividing it by the magnitude of $\vec v$.
Esta fórmula del coseno, tal cual, es la: This cosine formula, exactly as it stands, is the one used to decide whether two words mean similar things. Each word is represented by a vector counting which other words it appears with, and they are compared by angle and not by distance: that way a word ten times more frequent than another does not come out “far away” merely for being more frequent, because multiplying a vector by a positive number does not change its direction. It is called cosine similarity and it is in [[ia-vectores-palabras|words as vectors]].

Hay magnitudes que quedan definidas con: Some quantities are settled by a single number: mass, temperature, time. They are called scalars. But others also need a direction: velocity, force, a displacement. For those you need a vector: an arrow.

The little arrow on top is read “vector”: $\vec{v}$ is “vector v”. The two vertical bars, $|\vec{v}|$, are said “magnitude of v”, which is its length.

It reads: “vector v equals the pair v sub one, v sub two; and the magnitude of v is the square root of v sub one squared plus v sub two squared”.

The magnitude formula is not new: it is Pythagoras' theorem, with the components of the vector playing the part of the legs.

Llega una operación rara. Hasta ahora, a: Along comes a strange operation. Until now, operating with vectors gave vectors: you add one and another and get a vector. This one returns a number — that is why it is called scalar, which is what numbers are called when you want to tell them apart from vectors — and you have to understand first what that number measures, because otherwise the formula looks as if it came out of nowhere.
Lleva la punta a $(3, 4)$. ¿Cuánto medir: Take the tip to $(3, 4)$. What will the magnitude be? Think of the Pythagorean triple before looking.
Lo que mide es <strong>cuánto van los do: What it measures is how much the two vectors go the same way. Think of pushing a trolley. If you push exactly where you want it to go, all your effort counts. If you push a little sideways, only part of it is used. And if you push perpendicularly, down at the floor, the trolley does not move at all however tired you get: your effort does not count.
Los vectores tal como los usamos son sor: Vectors as we use them are surprisingly recent. They were born at the end of the nineteenth century out of an academic war: Hamilton had invented quaternions, an elegant but awkward system, and Gibbs and Heaviside separately extracted from them what physics really needed, the dot and cross products. Hamilton's supporters considered it a mutilation and the row lasted decades. The practical ones won, and that is why this is studied today and not that.

Para sumar dos vectores se suman sus com: To add two vectors you add their components. Geometrically, you put one after the other and the result runs from the start of the first to the finish of the second.

It reads: “the projection of u onto v is u dot v over the magnitude of v”.

It comes from the definition: $\vec u\cdot\vec v = |\vec u|\,|\vec v|\cos\alpha$, and the shadow measures $|\vec u|\cos\alpha$. If the angle is obtuse, the shadow falls backwards and comes out negative.

Un vector es la forma natural de decir «: A vector is the natural way of saying “how much and which way”, and so it appears the moment something has a direction: the wind pushing an aircraft off course, the current carrying a swimmer along, the force with which two people shove a piece of furniture. Adding vectors is what a pilot does when working out the heading needed to end up where they want despite a crosswind: the true course is the sum of their own and the air's.
